content.overview: A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) petition under Article 32 (Supreme Court) or Article 226 (High Court) is filed pro bono publico to vindicate the rights of the public or underprivileged groups unable to access courts due to poverty, ignorance, or disability.
content.short: A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) petition under Article 32 (Supreme Court) or Article 226 (High Court) is filed pro bono publico to vindicate the rights of the public or underprivileged groups unable to access courts due to poverty, ignorance, or disability.
content.detailed:
Core Drafting Skeleton & Checklist for PIL Petitions

1. Cause Title & Court of Jurisdiction
   • IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA (Civil Original Jurisdiction — Writ Petition under Article 32)
   • or IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT [City] (Extraordinary Civil Writ Jurisdiction under Article 226)

2. Memo of Parties & Standing (Locus Standi)
   • Petitioner: Full particulars + express declaration that petition is filed strictly as "pro bono publico" with zero personal, political, or oblique commercial profit/gain.
   • Respondents: Union of India / State Government, statutory commissions (e.g., NHRC, CPCB), and responsible nodal authorities.

3. Mandatory PIL Declarations (Balwant Singh Chaufal Compliance)
   • Means, standing, and credentials of the petitioner.
   • Statement of prior representation: Date and proof of notice/representation submitted to respondents demanding redressal, and failure of authority to act.
   • Confirmation that no other parallel petition on the identical subject matter is pending before any other court.

4. Statement of Facts & Class Impact
   • Clear narrative of the systemic wrong, environmental harm, or human rights violation.
   • Data, official survey reports, RTI disclosures, or judicial commission findings demonstrating broad public injury.

5. Legal Grounds & Constitutional Impugnment
   • Infringement of Part III rights (Arts 14, 19, 21, 21A, 23, 24).
   • Violation of statutory public duties and Directive Principles (Arts 39A, 47, 48A) read into Article 21.

6. Prayer Clause (Standard Public Law Remedies)
   • Writ of Mandamus directing authorities to enforce statutory mandates / formulate corrective guidelines.
   • Appointment of a Court-monitored Committee / Special Investigation Team (SIT) to supervise implementation.
   • Interim reliefs: immediate medical aid, suspension of toxic discharge, or interim living stipends.

7. Verification & Accompanying Affidavit of Bona Fides

Exam & Practice Highlights:
• Epistolary Jurisdiction: The SC/HC can treat a letter, telegram, or postcard from a victim or social activist as a writ petition.
• Non-Maintainable Sectors: PIL is expressly barred in service matters (seniority, promotions), tax assessment challenges, and private disputes.

cases.name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
cases.holding: Relaxed the strict rule of locus standi; any member of the public acting bona fide can invoke writ jurisdiction for a public wrong.
cases.relevance: Foundational charter of Public Interest Litigation in India.

cases.name: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
cases.holding: SC affirmed epistolary jurisdiction and appointed advocate-commissioners to inspect bonded stone quarries.
cases.relevance: Court inquiry commissions and procedural flexibility under Article 32(2).

cases.name: State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal
cases.holding: Laid down comprehensive 8-point mandatory guidelines for High Courts to filter frivolous, vexatious, or blackmailing PILs.
cases.relevance: Mandatory verification guidelines and costs for abuse of PIL process.

bareActPointers: State High Court PIL Rules & Practice Directions
examTips: Remember the three phases of PIL classified in Balwant Singh Chaufal (human rights, environment, governance/probity).
AIBE tests locus standi relaxation and non-maintainability of PILs in service matters.
Epistolary jurisdiction allows conversion of letters into formal writ petitions.
Always mention the mandatory declaration of bona fides and absence of personal gain in the opening paragraph.
